passages.t: Not one stone left on another: the disciples' question
passages.happening:
Jesus leaves the temple and is walking away when his disciples come to point out its buildings. “Do you see all these things?” he replies. “Truly I tell you, not one stone here will be left on another; every one will be thrown down” (verse 2).

Later, as Jesus sits on the Mount of Olives, the disciples come to him privately. “Tell us,” they say, “when will these things happen, and what will be the sign of Your coming and of the end of the age?” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this scene too (Mark 13:1-4), and the note on Mark 13 explains it. The disciples were not wrong to be impressed. Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple around 20 or 19 BC, and work went on for decades. The Jewish historian Josephus, who saw it, wrote that from a distance it looked like a mountain covered with snow, because the stone was so white (Jewish War 5.222-223). Within about forty years it was gone. In AD 70 a Roman army under Titus took Jerusalem, and the temple burned.

Matthew ties this chapter to the last one. Jesus has just said, ‘your house is left to you desolate’ (23:38). Now he walks out of the temple for the last time in Matthew's story, and says it will be thrown down.

Matthew also words the disciples' question his own way. In Mark they ask when ‘these things’ will happen. In Matthew they ask about two things: the fall of the temple, and ‘Your coming and the end of the age’. The word for ‘coming’ is parousia. In ordinary Greek it meant someone's arrival or presence, and it was used of the official visit of a king or emperor to a city. Among the Gospels only Matthew uses it, and only in this chapter (verses 3, 27, 37 and 39). The disciples may have thought the temple's fall and the end of the world were one event. Much of the chapter is about telling them apart.
passages.ot: Jesus was not the first Jew to say the temple would fall. Centuries earlier the prophet Micah had said, “Jerusalem will become a heap of rubble” (Micah 3:12), and Jeremiah warned the people not to trust in the building as if it made them safe (Jeremiah 7:4). The first temple, built by Solomon, was destroyed by Babylon. Jesus speaks in the line of those prophets.
passages.hard:
How should this chapter be read? Christians have read it in three main ways. Some read most of it as about the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, told in the prophets' picture-language. Some read most of it as about the end of the age and Christ's return. Many read it as about both: the near event as a picture of the final one, with the line between them drawn somewhere in the chapter. Christians who hold each view confess together in the creeds that Christ will come again in glory. These notes leave the question of which verses describe which event open, and they offer no end-times timetable.

Was this a prophecy, or written after the event? Some scholars think the Gospels were written after AD 70, so the words could reflect what had already happened. Others note that the chapter gives none of the details of the siege and think the saying goes back to Jesus. Either way, a prophet saying the temple would fall was not new in Israel.
passages.asks: The disciples looked at the stones and felt safe. Jesus looked at the same stones and saw how short their life was. Ask what in your life looks permanent: a job, a church building, a country, your own strength. Jesus does not ask you to despise those things. He asks you not to rest your whole weight on them.

passages.t: Do not be deceived, do not be alarmed
passages.happening:
Jesus does not begin with a date. He begins with a warning: “See to it that no one deceives you” (verse 4). Many will come in his name, saying, ‘I am the Christ’, and will fool many. There will be wars and rumours of wars, “but see to it that you are not alarmed” (verse 6). These things must happen, but the end is still to come. Nations will rise against nations. There will be famines and earthquakes. “All these are the beginning of birth pains” (verse 8).

Then his followers will be handed over, persecuted and killed, and hated by all nations because of his name. Many will fall away and betray one another. False prophets will lead many astray. Because wickedness multiplies, the love of most will grow cold. “But the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (verse 13). And this gospel of the kingdom will be preached in all the world as a testimony to all nations, “and then the end will come” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Mark has this passage too (Mark 13:5-13), and the note on Mark 13 explains it. The first readers did not need to imagine any of it. In the years after Jesus, men rose up in Judea promising signs of rescue. Josephus tells of one named Theudas, who around AD 45 promised to part the Jordan River (Antiquities 20.97-98), and the book of Acts mentions him (Acts 5:36). Roman soldiers scattered such movements.

Birth pains were a picture the prophets used. Labour pain is real, and once it begins it cannot be stopped. But it is the pain of something being born. The troubles are real and hard, and they are not the end of the story.

Matthew adds some lines of his own. He warns that the love of most will grow cold. And he says that the good news, which Jesus once sent the Twelve to take only to Israel (10:5-6), will be preached to all nations before the end. Matthew's Gospel ends with that very command: “make disciples of all nations” (28:19).
passages.ot:
Isaiah used the picture of birth pains for Israel's suffering before God's rescue: “As a woman with child about to give birth writhes and cries out in pain” (Isaiah 26:17).

The split inside families and among friends echoes Micah, who mourned a time when “a man's enemies are the members of his own household” (Micah 7:6).
passages.hard:
Every age has had wars, earthquakes and famines, and in every age someone has said they prove the end is here. Jesus says the opposite. “These things must happen, but the end is still to come” (verse 6). They are not a countdown. They are the normal weather of a broken world, and Jesus tells his followers not to be alarmed by them.

If the news frightens you, or you were taught as a child to dread the end of the world, notice the first thing Jesus says after the wars: ‘see to it that you are not alarmed’. He does not hand his followers a chart to watch. He tells them to stay faithful, keep loving, and keep telling the good news.
passages.asks: The first danger Jesus names is not war. It is being fooled. Ask who you let tell you what the news means, and whether fear makes you easier to fool. Then ask about your love. Has it grown cold in a hard season? Jesus' answer to a dark world is not panic but perseverance, and good news carried to every nation.

passages.t: The abomination of desolation, and false Christs
passages.happening:
Jesus gives a sign. “So when you see standing in the holy place ‘the abomination of desolation,’ described by the prophet Daniel (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains” (verses 15-16). A man on the roof must not go down for anything in his house. A man in the field must not go back for his cloak. It will be terribly hard for pregnant women and nursing mothers. “Pray that your flight will not occur in the winter or on the Sabbath” (verse 20). There will be great distress, worse than any before or after, and for the sake of God's chosen ones those days will be cut short.

Then a warning again. If anyone says, “Look, here is the Christ!” do not believe it. False Christs and false prophets will do great signs to deceive even the chosen, if that were possible. Do not go out into the wilderness to look for him, or into the inner rooms. “For just as the lightning comes from the east and flashes as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (verse 27). “Wherever there is a carcass, there the vultures will gather” (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
Mark has this passage too (Mark 13:14-23), and the note on Mark 13 explains it. An abomination is something disgusting to God, usually an idol. ‘The abomination of desolation’ means a horrible thing that leaves the holy place empty and ruined. Around 167 BC the Greek king Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar in the temple, and the Jewish book of 1 Maccabees calls it by this very name (1 Maccabees 1:54). Around AD 40 the emperor Caligula ordered a statue of himself set up in the temple. He was murdered in January 41 before it was done. So the phrase named a real fear.

Matthew makes three things plainer than Mark. He names Daniel. He says where the horror will stand: ‘in the holy place’, the temple. And he adds the Sabbath to the prayer about winter. The law told Israel that on the seventh day “everyone must stay where he is; no one may leave his place” (Exodus 16:29). For people who kept the Sabbath, as Matthew's first readers very likely did, a flight on that day would be a hard thing. Jesus thinks of that too.

The church historian Eusebius, writing in the early 300s, reports that the Christians of Jerusalem were warned and left the city before the war, settling at Pella, east of the Jordan (Church History 3.5.3). Historians debate how much of that story is history. But it shows that early Christians took this warning as practical advice to run.

Mark does not have the lightning, though Luke does (Luke 17:24). The true coming of the Son of Man will not be a rumour whispered in a back room. It will be as plain as lightning across the whole sky. No one will need to be told where he is.

Verse 28 sounds like a common saying: where there is a dead body, the birds gather. The Greek word can mean ‘eagles’ or ‘vultures’. Some readers think of the eagle standards of the Roman legions gathering around a dying Jerusalem. Others take it simply to mean that when the time comes, it will be as plain as birds circling over a carcass.
passages.ot:
Daniel speaks of this horror set up in the temple. In Daniel 11:31 an enemy's forces “will rise up and desecrate the temple fortress. They will abolish the daily sacrifice and set up the abomination of desolation” (see also Daniel 9:27 and 12:11).

The great distress echoes Daniel too, who speaks of “a time of distress, the likes of which will not have occurred from the beginning of nations until that time” (Daniel 12:1).

The birds and the dead are an old picture. Job says of the eagle, “where the slain are, there he is” (Job 39:30).
passages.hard:
What exactly is the abomination? Christians have given three main answers, each with careful defenders.

Some read it as the Roman armies and the events that led to the temple's destruction in AD 70. On this view, the warning to flee was for the people of Judea in that generation, and Luke's version supports it, since Luke says, “when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies” (Luke 21:20).

Others read it as still in the future, a final enemy of God before Christ returns. Readers who hold this often link it with Paul's words about a man of lawlessness who sets himself up in God's temple (2 Thessalonians 2:3-4).

Many read it both ways: fulfilled in AD 70, and also a pattern of what will come again before the end.

These notes do not choose among them. All three agree on what Jesus actually tells his followers to do: do not be fooled, do not stay to save your things, and trust God, who limits the days. And whoever claims to be Christ come back in secret, or tells you where to go to find him, is not to be believed.
passages.asks: Jesus' advice in the crisis is surprising. He does not say stay and fight. He says run, and do not go back for your things. Ask what you would cling to if you had to leave everything. Notice too that he thinks of pregnant women and nursing mothers, and of people who keep the Sabbath, in the middle of a speech about the end. His eye goes to the most vulnerable.

passages.t: The Son of Man coming on the clouds
passages.happening:
“Immediately after the tribulation of those days,” Jesus says, the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, the stars will fall from the sky, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken (verse 29).

“At that time the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn” (verse 30). They will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. He will send out his angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather his chosen ones from the four winds, from one end of the heavens to the other.
passages.hearers:
Mark has this passage too (Mark 13:24-27), and the note on Mark 13 explains it. This is the language of the prophets. They used pictures of a darkened sun and falling stars when God brought down a great power within history. Isaiah used them for the fall of Babylon (Isaiah 13:10). A first-century Jew would not take these words as a weather report. Nor would he think they were only decoration. They meant that God was acting in a way that would shake the world.

Matthew adds three things: the sign of the Son of Man, the mourning of the tribes, and the trumpet.

What is ‘the sign of the Son of Man’? Readers differ. Many think the sign is the Son of Man himself, appearing in the sky. John Chrysostom, a preacher of the late 300s, took it to be the cross, shining brighter than the sun (Homily 76 on Matthew). Matthew does not explain it.

In Israel trumpets were blown at the feasts and to call the people together (Numbers 10:10).
passages.ot:
Daniel saw “One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven.” He came to the Ancient of Days, God himself, and “He was given dominion, glory, and kingship” (Daniel 7:13-14).

The mourning tribes echo Zechariah: “they will look on Me, the One they have pierced. They will mourn for Him as one mourns for an only child” (Zechariah 12:10). In Zechariah it is the mourning of people who see what they have done, and it comes with ‘a spirit of grace and prayer’.

The great trumpet echoes Isaiah: “And in that day a great ram’s horn will sound,” and the scattered exiles come home to worship (Isaiah 27:13). And Moses promised that even if Israel were banished to the farthest horizon, “He will gather you and return you from there” (Deuteronomy 30:4).
passages.hard:
Does this passage describe the end of history, or the events of AD 70?

Many Christians read verses 29 to 31 as the second coming of Christ at the end of the age, when he returns in glory and gathers his people. This has been the most common reading through the centuries.

Others read the passage as describing the fall of Jerusalem in the prophets' picture-language. In Daniel, the Son of Man comes to God, not down to earth, to receive a kingdom. On this view, the temple's fall showed that Jesus had been given that kingdom. Those who read it this way still believe Christ will return, and they find that promise in verses 36 to 51 and elsewhere in the New Testament.

Still others think both are in view, the near event as a picture of the final one.

Christians who hold each of these views confess together in the creeds that Christ will come again in glory. They differ on which verses describe which event. These notes leave that question open, and they offer no end-times timetable.
passages.asks: Jesus does not end with falling stars. He ends with a gathering. The last word is not chaos but his people brought home from every corner of the earth, as the trumpet once called the exiles home. Ask whether you think about the future mostly with fear or mostly with hope, and which one this passage invites.

passages.happening:
Jesus says, “Now learn this lesson from the fig tree” (verse 32). As soon as its branches become tender and sprout leaves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see all these things, you will know that he is near, right at the door.

Then he makes a solemn promise: “Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened” (verse 34). And he adds, “Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away” (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Mark has this passage almost word for word (Mark 13:28-31), and the note on Mark 13 explains it. Many trees in the land of Israel, such as the olive, keep their leaves all year. The fig tree does not. It stands bare through winter, and its new leaves come late. So when a fig tree put out tender leaves, everyone knew summer was close. It was a sign anyone could read.

The word ‘generation’ in Greek is genea. In Matthew it usually means the people alive in Jesus' day. Just one chapter before, Jesus said that the judgment he warned of “will come upon this generation” (23:36).

The disciples had already seen one fig tree in this part of the story, the one that withered (21:19). This one is a sign of hope: leaves mean summer is coming.
passages.ot: Jesus' last promise sounds like Isaiah: “The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever” (Isaiah 40:8). Isaiah said that about the word of God. Jesus says it about his own words.
passages.hard:
Verse 34 is one of the hardest in the Bible. If ‘all these things’ includes the coming of the Son of Man, did Jesus promise that the end would come within his hearers' lifetimes? Many skeptics have said yes, and that he was wrong. The objection is serious, and Christians have felt it too. C. S. Lewis, a believer, called this saying ‘the most embarrassing verse in the Bible’ in his essay The World's Last Night. Matthew makes the question sharper, since the disciples asked about his ‘coming’ (verse 3) and the coming follows ‘immediately after’ the distress (verse 29).

Christians have answered in three main ways.

One reading says that ‘all these things’ means the signs and the fall of the temple, which did happen within about forty years. The coming itself is ‘that day’ in verse 36, which no one knows. Readers who hold this point out that in verse 33 ‘all these things’ are signs seen before he is near, so they cannot include his coming.

A second reading says that the whole passage up to verse 35 describes AD 70, read in the prophets' picture-language, and was fulfilled within that generation.

A third reading takes ‘this generation’ in another sense, such as the generation that sees the signs, or the Jewish people, or even the kind of people who resist God.

Each view has a weakness its critics point to, and careful Christians hold each one. When Jesus will return is a question on which faithful Christians differ. That he will return is confessed by all.
passages.asks: Jesus stakes everything on his words. Heaven and earth will go, but what he has said will stand. Ask whose words you trust most when you are afraid: the news, your own feelings, or his. A fig tree teaches you to notice. Jesus wants his followers awake to what God is doing, not scanning the sky for a date.

passages.t: No one knows the day or hour: as in the days of Noah
passages.happening:
“No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father” (verse 36).

It will be as it was in Noah's day. Before the flood, people were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, up to the day Noah went into the ark. They knew nothing until the flood came and swept them all away. So it will be when the Son of Man comes. Two men will be in the field: one will be taken and the other left. Two women will be grinding at the mill: one will be taken and the other left.

“Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day on which your Lord will come” (verse 42). If a homeowner had known when the thief was coming, he would have stayed awake. “For this reason, you also must be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect” (verse 44).
passages.hearers:
Mark has the saying about the day and hour (Mark 13:32). Matthew adds Noah, the two in the field and at the mill, and the thief. Luke has some of these sayings in another place (Luke 17:26-37).

Notice what the people in Noah's day were doing. Eating, drinking and marrying are not sins. They are ordinary life. The danger Jesus names is not that people were living normally, but that they lived as if nothing would ever change and God would never act.

Grinding grain was a daily job, done by hand on a heavy stone mill, and women often did it together. Bread was at least half of what ordinary people ate. Jesus pictures the end coming in the middle of an ordinary working day.

A thief does not send word ahead. The early Christians took up this picture: Paul wrote that “the Day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians 5:2).
passages.ot: In Genesis the flood came on a world full of wickedness (Genesis 6:5), and “only Noah and those with him in the ark remained” (Genesis 7:23). Noah was not saved by guessing the date. He was ready because he did what God told him.
passages.hard:
How can the Son not know the day, if he is God? In the 300s the followers of Arius used words like these to argue that the Son was a lesser being than the Father. The church leader Athanasius answered that Jesus spoke this way as a true human being. The Son had taken on a full human life, with its real limits, as Luke says he “grew in wisdom” (Luke 2:52). The church later confessed at the Council of Chalcedon, in 451, that Christ is truly God and truly man in one person. How best to describe what Jesus knew in his earthly life is still something Christians discuss. Some later copies of Matthew leave out ‘nor the Son’, but the oldest manuscripts have it, and so does Mark.

This verse also stands against every attempt to set a date for the end. Many have tried, and every one has been wrong. If the Son did not give a date, no preacher, chart or book can. Jesus told his disciples again after his resurrection, “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by His own authority” (Acts 1:7).

What does ‘one will be taken and the other left’ mean? Christians read it in two main ways. Many read it as the rapture: believers are suddenly taken to be with Christ, and others are left behind. The word rapture comes from the Latin for ‘caught up’ in 1 Thessalonians 4:17, “we who are alive and remain will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air.” Others read it the opposite way. In Noah's day it was the people swept away by the flood who were taken, in judgment, and Noah who was left, safe. Luke's version adds the disciples' question, ‘Where, Lord?’, and Jesus' answer about vultures gathering at a body (Luke 17:37), which points to judgment. Christians also differ on when such a taking happens and how it fits with other passages. These notes do not choose, and they set out no end-times scheme. Both readings agree on Jesus' own point: the coming will be sudden, it will divide people who stood side by side, and the only wise thing is to be ready now.
passages.asks: If end-times teaching has frightened you, or you were taught to fear being ‘left behind’, notice what Jesus actually asks. Not to work out a timetable. Not to live in dread. He asks you to be ready, and being ready means trusting him and doing the work he has given you today. Ask what ‘ready’ would look like in your ordinary week: in the field, at the mill, at home.

passages.t: The faithful servant and the wicked servant
passages.happening:
Jesus asks, “Who then is the faithful and wise servant, whom the master has put in charge of his household, to give the others their food at the proper time?” (verse 45). Blessed is that servant whose master finds him doing so when he returns. The master will put him in charge of everything he owns.

But suppose the servant is wicked and says to himself, ‘My master will be away a long time.’ He begins to beat his fellow servants and to eat and drink with drunkards. The master will come on a day he does not expect and at an hour he does not know. He will cut him to pieces and give him a place with the hypocrites, “where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (verse 51).
passages.hearers:
In the story the master puts one servant in charge of his household while he is away, to hand out the food to the others. Luke tells this parable too (Luke 12:42-46).

Notice what the faithful servant is doing when the master comes: feeding the others, on time. Not watching the road. Not guessing the date. Just doing his job well.

Notice what the wicked servant's sin is. He decides the master is not coming soon, and so he can treat the others however he likes. Waiting turns into abuse of power. The ones he beats are his ‘fellow servants’, people in his care.

‘Cut him to pieces’ is a fierce phrase, and readers differ on whether it pictures a terrible punishment or being cut off from the household. Either way, the wicked servant ends ‘with the hypocrites’, the word Jesus used again and again in chapter 23 for religious leaders whose lives did not match their words.
passages.ot: Ezekiel's woe fits this servant exactly: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves! Should not the shepherds feed their flock?” (Ezekiel 34:2). And Isaiah spoke of watchmen posted on the walls of Jerusalem who are never silent, day or night (Isaiah 62:6). Watching was a job, not a mood.
passages.asks: This parable is first for those who lead in the church: pastors, teachers, anyone put in charge of others. Ask whether you are feeding the people in your care, or using them. And for every reader, ask what you would want the master to find you doing if he came today. If the honest answer is the work you are already doing, faithfully and kindly, then you are ready.
